questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the **intensity** of light of a fixed frequency (above threshold) increases:
options: The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
The number of electrons emitted per second
questions.solution:
Einstein's equation is $K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$ — the maximum kinetic energy depends on **frequency** alone.

Greater intensity means more photons per second, so **more electrons per second**, but each electron still absorbs exactly one photon of the same energy.

This is precisely what the wave theory could not explain, and why the effect established the photon.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment the fringe width is:
questions.solution:
$\beta = \mathbf{\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}}$, where $D$ is the slit-to-screen distance and $d$ the slit separation.

So the fringes widen with longer wavelength or a more distant screen, and narrow as the slits are moved apart. Immersing the apparatus in water shortens $\lambda$ and so **narrows** the fringes.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum $p$ is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \mathbf{\dfrac{h}{p}}$.

Because $h$ is so small ($6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$), everyday objects have utterly unobservable wavelengths. An electron accelerated through a few tens of volts, however, has $\lambda$ of about an ångström — comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electrons diffract off crystals.

questions.q: The power of a lens of focal length $f$ (in metres) is:
questions.solution:
$P = \mathbf{\dfrac{1}{f}}$, measured in dioptres when $f$ is in metres.

A converging lens has positive power, a diverging one negative. Powers of lenses in contact simply **add**, which is why they are used rather than focal lengths.

questions.q: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, the energy of the $n$th level is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$E_n = \mathbf{-\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}}$.

The negative sign means the electron is bound; the levels crowd together towards $E = 0$ as $n$ grows, which is the ionisation limit.

The radius goes the other way, $r_n \propto n^{2}$.

questions.q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels:
options: From a rarer to a denser medium at any angle
From a denser to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle
questions.solution:
Two conditions are both needed: the light must go from a **denser to a rarer** medium, and the angle of incidence must **exceed the critical angle** $C$, where $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{\mu}$.

This is what makes optical fibres work, and it is why a diamond ($\mu = 2.42$, so $C \approx 24^\circ$) sparkles — light entering it is trapped through many internal reflections.

questions.q: The binding energy per nucleon is greatest for nuclei of mass number around:
questions.solution:
The binding energy per nucleon peaks near $A \approx \mathbf{56}$ — iron and nickel — at about $8.8\ \text{MeV}$ per nucleon.

That peak is why **fusion** of light nuclei and **fission** of heavy ones both release energy: each moves the products towards the most tightly bound region of the curve. It is also why iron is the end of the line for stellar fusion.

questions.q: For single-slit diffraction, the first minimum occurs at angle $\theta$ where:
questions.solution:
The **minima** of single-slit diffraction are at $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ for $n = 1, 2, 3\ldots$, so the first is at $\mathbf{a\sin\theta = \lambda}$.

Be careful: in the double-slit experiment the same expression gives the **maxima**. The two are easily confused and the distinction is worth memorising.

questions.q: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment depends on:
questions.solution:
$eV_0 = K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$, so the stopping potential depends on the **frequency** of the light (and the metal's work function), not on its intensity.

A graph of $V_0$ against $\nu$ is a straight line of slope $h/e$ — the experiment Millikan used to measure Planck's constant.

questions.q: Light of energy $5\ \text{eV}$ falls on a metal of work function $2\ \text{eV}$. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in electronvolts.
In a double-slit experiment, $\lambda = 600\ \text{nm}$, $d = 0.3\ \text{mm}$ and $D = 1\ \text{m}$. Find the fringe width, in millimetres.
Find the energy of the $n = 2$ level of hydrogen, in electronvolts. Give the magnitude.
questions.solution:
$E_2 = -\dfrac{13.6}{2^{2}} = -\dfrac{13.6}{4} = -3.4\ \text{eV}$.

The magnitude is $\mathbf{3.4\ \text{eV}}$ — the energy needed to ionise hydrogen from its first excited state.

questions.q: A medium has refractive index $2$. Find its critical angle, in degrees.
An electron is accelerated through $150\ \text{V}$. Using $\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$, find its de Broglie wavelength in ångström, to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\sqrt{150} \approx 12.25$

$\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{12.25} \approx \mathbf{1.00\ \text{Å}}$.

That is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is exactly why electrons of this energy are diffracted by one — the Davisson-Germer experiment.

questions.q: State the laws of the photoelectric effect and explain why the classical wave theory of light fails to account for them. Write Einstein's photoelectric equation and describe how a graph of stopping potential against frequency is used to find Planck's constant.
questions.solution:
**The experimental laws.**

1. Emission is **instantaneous** — there is no measurable delay, even for very faint light.
2. There is a **threshold frequency** $\nu_0$ below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light or however long it shines.
3. The **maximum kinetic energy** of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency of the light and on the metal, but **not at all on the intensity**.
4. The **number** of electrons emitted per second is proportional to the **intensity**.

**Why the wave theory fails.** On the classical picture, light is a wave whose energy is spread continuously over the wavefront and is carried by the intensity.

- **Against law 1:** an electron would have to **accumulate** energy from the wave. For faint light the calculation gives delays of hours; experiment finds less than $10^{-9}\ \text{s}$.
- **Against law 2:** there should be **no threshold**. Light of any frequency, given enough intensity or enough time, ought eventually to supply the required energy. It does not.
- **Against law 3:** a more intense wave carries more energy, so it should eject **faster** electrons. It does not — it ejects **more** of them at the same maximum speed.

The failure is not a matter of detail. The wave theory gets the **dependence on the wrong variable**: it makes everything hinge on intensity, and the experiment makes the crucial things hinge on frequency.

**Einstein's explanation.** Light is absorbed in discrete quanta — **photons** — each of energy $h\nu$. One electron absorbs one whole photon, all at once.

Part of that energy is spent freeing the electron from the metal (the **work function** $\phi$); the rest appears as kinetic energy:

$\boxed{h\nu = \phi + K_{\max}}$

or $K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$.

Every law now follows immediately:

- One photon, one electron, one absorption event — so emission is **instantaneous**.
- If $h\nu < \phi$ no single photon can free an electron, whatever the number of them — hence the **threshold**, $\nu_0 = \phi/h$.
- $K_{\max}$ contains $\nu$ and not the intensity.
- Greater intensity is simply more photons, so more electrons.

**Measuring $h$.** Applying a reverse potential $V_0$ just large enough to stop the fastest electrons gives

$eV_0 = K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi$

$V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$

Measure $V_0$ for several frequencies and plot $V_0$ against $\nu$. The result is a **straight line**, and:

- the **slope** is $\dfrac{h}{e}$, so $h = e \times \text{slope}$;
- the **intercept on the $\nu$ axis** is the threshold frequency $\nu_0$;
- the **intercept on the $V_0$ axis** is $-\dfrac{\phi}{e}$, giving the work function.

The decisive point is that the slope comes out the **same for every metal**, even though the intercepts differ. That is what shows $h$ to be a universal constant of nature and not a property of the particular surface — and it is the measurement for which Millikan, who had set out to disprove Einstein's equation, ended up confirming it.
